Introduction/Organisation transformation

Development guide

Organisation transformation

Introducing AI tools changes more than how a team drafts code. Someone still needs to define the task, check the result and decide whether it can be used. When drafting becomes faster, unclear requirements or limited review capacity can become more visible.

This chapter helps team leads and delivery teams plan those changes across people, process, culture and technology. Start with one recurring problem, identify the supporting changes and use a small pilot to decide whether the proposed workflow helps.

AI-assisted development means using AI to support development work. The resulting software does not need to contain AI.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Support learning
  • Prepare review evidence
  • Learn from failures
  • Test bounded delegation

Why the way of working needs to change

AI tooling can help a team draft code faster, but organisational transformation means improving how the whole team delivers useful, reliable software. If requirements remain unclear, reviewers are unavailable or release decisions are delayed, faster coding can simply move more work into a queue. The tool changes one activity; the organisation needs to connect that capability to the rest of delivery.

That requires changes across four areas. People need the skills and time to specify tasks and judge AI-generated work. Process needs clear ownership, checks and decision points so that work can move forward. Culture needs to support questioning outputs, reporting failures and improving the workflow. Technology needs suitable context, test environments and access controls to support those practices. Each area depends on the others: trained reviewers need time in the process, and a failed check is useful only when someone can raise it and act on it.

Start with one recurring delay or quality problem, then trial the tool alongside the changes needed in those four areas. Compare the time to an accepted result, review and rework effort, and defects before expanding the trial. Use the four-area planning questions to shape the change and the pilot measures to judge whether it helps.

Supporting evidence: workflow redesign and AI productivity

DORA’s 2025 report describes AI as amplifying existing organisational strengths and weaknesses.

McKinsey’s November 2025 survey found that respondents in its AI high-performer group were nearly three times as likely as others to report fundamental workflow redesign. That group reported both significant AI value and an AI contribution of at least 5% to earnings before interest and taxes. This self-reported association does not establish that redesign caused the results.

Measure the effect in your own setting. METR’s early-2025 randomised study of 16 experienced open-source developers, completing 246 tasks in familiar repositories, found that allowing AI tools increased completion time by 19%. Participants nevertheless estimated that AI had saved them time.

That result is specific to those tools, tasks and developers. In February 2026, METR reported that selection effects and time-measurement problems made its follow-up data unreliable for estimating current productivity gains. Neither study supplies a forecast for your squad.

Sources: [1]; [2]; [3]; [4].

Four areas that change together

Use people, process, culture and technology to plan connected changes.

The four areas apply to the same task. The example below shows how a team could address them together in a small pilot.

Example · fictional upload-feature pilot

An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions and limits. In this pilot, a team asks an agent to help build a document upload feature on an isolated branch, using synthetic documents and simulated recipients.

  • People: the product owner and developer agree a task brief describing the intended user, upload behaviour and access limits. They name reviewers with time to check the code, tests and security implications.
  • Process: the team defines checks before coding: an allowed upload succeeds, an unsupported file is rejected and an unauthorised recipient cannot receive a document. Reviewers record the results; the person authorised to accept the change records the decision and any unresolved issues.
  • Culture: if the agent misses an access check, the developer raises the problem for discussion. The team examines the instructions and review process, then records a correction, who will make it and when it will be checked.
  • Technology: the platform engineer provides separate test storage and limits the agent to the branch and test environment. The developer and platform engineer test how to stop the agent, revoke its access and restore the test environment. The agent cannot merge changes or deploy to production.
Questions to answer before a pilot
AreaPlanning questionUseful output
PeopleWho can specify, perform and review the task?Named participants, skill gaps and coaching time
ProcessWhat evidence supports progress, and who decides?A task flow with checks and decision authority
CultureHow will people raise concerns and learn from failures?A feedback route and a review date
TechnologyWhat can the tool access, change and recover?Access limits, action records and a recovery method

Use the agent guidance below when an AI tool can take actions, such as changing files or running commands in a system.

People: develop skills and organise responsibilities

AI-assisted work still needs people who understand the user’s problem and can recognise an incorrect result. Build enough shared knowledge for colleagues to work across tasks, while preserving access to specialist review.

Develop breadth alongside depth

A T-shaped practitioner combines deep expertise in one field with enough breadth to collaborate across the lifecycle. Use this as a development goal, not an expectation that one person can replace a multidisciplinary team.

Observe the practice: breadth means a developer can trace one user requirement through implementation, testing and operational evidence, and recognise when to ask for help. Depth means a security specialist can explain a failed access-control test and verify the correction.

Make review responsibilities explicit

For each change, agree who specifies the user need, carries out the work and reviews the result. Identify the evidence each reviewer needs and the person authorised to accept the change. Use the role examples below to plan skills and review capacity; map them to the organisation’s existing responsibilities.

Quality assurance (QA) and security collaborate, but answer different questions. QA assesses whether behaviour and reliability meet agreed criteria; security assesses threats and the effectiveness of protective controls. Record their acceptance responsibilities separately under the existing process. A QA acceptance does not grant security approval, and a security review does not establish functional acceptance. Route unresolved risks to the person authorised to accept them.

Learn through supported practice

Reserve time for coached work on a low-risk task. Pair a learner with someone able to review the result, and include a flawed output so the learner can practise detecting errors. Assess the specification, verification and explanation of limits, as well as the completed work.

Team leads can collect recurring skill gaps; whoever coordinates training can use that evidence to arrange coaching and share worked examples. Avoid treating tool usage or course completion alone as proof of competence.

AIHow AI can help

Use AI to draft alternative approaches to a low-risk practice task and explain its assumptions. A learner and coach check the results against the agreed criteria, identify errors and record the skill to practise next. Assess the review as well as the finished work.

Organise delegated work and review capacity

Delegating a task to an agent changes who produces the first result and what reviewers need to inspect. People define the outcome and permitted actions, then check the returned work and decide whether it can be used. Agents can carry out bounded research, prototyping, coding or test generation; organisational accountability remains with people.

For a material decision, reviewers should form an independent view before accepting an agent-supported recommendation. Ask three questions: what result did we expect and what alternative explanation could be true; which direct user observation, test or system evidence supports the conclusion; and what remains uncertain, including who owns the decision. This recommended check focuses scrutiny on consequential decisions; it does not create a universal human-approval step.

The diagram uses product owner (PO), business analyst (BA), technical lead, developer, platform engineer and QA and security reviewer as example contributors. Choose the task owner and reviewers from the roles involved in the work.

Name the person delegating each task and the person authorised to accept its result. Retain the changed files, test results and unresolved questions for review. Assign work according to the team’s capacity to check it; the diagram’s roles and agent capabilities are examples, not a staffing ratio.

Build on existing expertise

AI-assisted work adds responsibilities to established professional expertise. Use the examples below to agree development needs for the work each person actually does. Assess competence through observed decisions and reviewed outputs.

The examples use “product owner” for the person clarifying a change’s user need, scope and acceptance criteria. Where product management and product ownership are separate roles, agree their contributions under the existing process rather than treating the titles as interchangeable. A business analyst may help investigate needs and specify requirements; that contribution does not itself grant acceptance authority.

Agree who maintains the instructions, tools, permissions and checks around the agent. Together, these form its agent harness. For interface work, designers can supply named values for colour, typography and spacing, called design tokens, to guide generated screens.

Existing expertise, additional responsibilities and observable competence.
RoleExisting expertiseAdditional responsibilitiesObservable work
Product ownerUser needs, scope, prioritisation and acceptance criteriaClarify intent for AI-assisted tasks; define evaluation criteria and exclusions.Identifies a flawed specification, resolves conflicting needs and rejects an outcome claim based on incomplete evidence.
UI/UX designerUser research, interaction design, accessibility and usability evaluationEvaluate generated experiences and failure states; guide prototypes with design tokens.Finds a misleading interaction or accessibility failure and tests the correction with relevant users.
Technical leadArchitecture, system trade-offs, engineering guidance and code reviewReview agent task boundaries, integration risks and the suitability of the harness.Detects an unsafe permission boundary, requests missing evidence and involves a security or platform specialist when needed.
DeveloperSoftware design, implementation, debugging, testing and operationsSpecify bounded tasks; inspect agent actions; verify changes against requirements.Finds a specification error repeated in generated code and tests, checks the correction and escalates beyond their expertise.
Platform / Cloud EngineerContinuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) automation, cloud infrastructure, networking, identity, hardening, monitoring and service recoveryReview AI-generated pipeline and infrastructure changes; bound deployment permissions; maintain automated controls and operational visibility.Rejects an over-permissive deployment change, demonstrates a blocked pipeline check, verifies infrastructure hardening and tests that an application failure triggers an actionable alert and recovery procedure.
QA specialistTest strategy, exploratory testing, reliability and defect analysisMaintain evaluation cases for AI-assisted work; assess generated tests and gaps in evidence.Identifies a missing failure case, reproduces a defect and records whether quality acceptance criteria are met.
Security specialistThreat modelling, access control, security testing and risk assessmentAssess agent tools, data flows and isolation controls, including attempts to redirect an agent through instructions in untrusted content (prompt injection).Demonstrates an unsafe permission boundary, verifies the control and routes residual risk to the authorised decision-maker.

Include Platform / Cloud Engineer capacity from planning through operation, either within the squad or through a named shared platform team. Agree the boundary between shared infrastructure and application responsibilities, with a support route and deputy. Developers add application health signals and diagnose code failures; platform engineers maintain the delivery and monitoring foundations. QA checks behaviour and reliability; security reviews threats and controls. Release and risk decisions follow the existing authorities.

Everyone needs to recognise incomplete evidence and know when to involve a specialist. Multi-agent orchestration is an optional specialism for people whose tasks require it; it is not a mastery target for every developer. Assign it with time for integration, review and recovery.

For document definitions, see the PRD and TRD guidance: the product requirements document (PRD) describes the required outcomes; the technical requirements document (TRD) records how the system will deliver them. Who prepares and approves these records depends on the applicable workflow. Follow the Eitri planning steps when using that implementation.

Practise delegation on one task

Start with a task whose outcome the team can check. Agree the permitted actions, arrange review capacity and use a pilot to assess whether the arrangement helps. Keep the scope small while the team learns.

  1. Discuss the table with each squad member, and agree one additional responsibility to practise and the work that will demonstrate competence.
  2. Start with advice-only or isolated tasks, where a person reviews every result.
  3. Pair each learner with someone who can review their work; for example, a technical lead checking a proposed implementation against the requirements and access limits.
  4. Widen an agent’s scope only when the evidence supports it and the person with authority agrees.

Example · fictional upload-feature review

In the upload-feature pilot, the developer gives the agent the agreed upload behaviour and recipient-access rules. The agent drafts a change and tests on the isolated branch. The developer compares both with the requirements and finds that neither checks whether the selected recipient is authorised.

The developer records the gap and reproduces the failure, then corrects the task instructions and asks the agent to revise the change. After checking the correction, the developer retains the failed and passing test results. A security reviewer examines the access-control evidence, and the technical lead reviews the integrated change. These are the fictional team’s chosen review arrangements; acceptance follows the existing decision authority.

The platform engineer retains pipeline results and confirms that the agent cannot merge or deploy. The pilot lead records the review and correction effort, including the failed attempt, for the comparison at the end of this chapter.

If several agents work on separate tasks, plan time to integrate and review their results. Tests generated from the same misunderstood requirement can repeat the implementation error. Additional agents do not remove the need for an independent check against the intended behaviour.

Choose team size and specialist coverage from workload, risk and review capacity. Smaller teams and greater agent autonomy are not measures of maturity.

Next step: with each squad member, pick the table row closest to their role. Agree one additional responsibility to practise on the next low-risk task, what evidence will demonstrate it and who will review the result.

Process: connect checks to decisions

Map the existing workflow before changing it. Separate time spent doing work from time waiting for information, review or approval. A slow checkpoint may need clearer inputs or more review capacity, rather than automation.

Keep the purpose of each control visible

  1. Ask the person responsible for the control what outcome it protects.
  2. Record the evidence needed and which checks can assess it reliably.
  3. Confirm who can authorise progress and when a person needs to intervene.

A passing check provides evidence for the authorised decision. Record acceptance or rework with its reason; unresolved failures do not become a pass. Review lessons before changing rules or thresholds.

Set authority for the specific task

Choose agent permissions according to impact, reversibility and the evidence available. IMDA’s Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI recommends risk limits, human accountability and lifecycle controls. The table below gives this guide’s local task-boundary examples.

Example task permissions; these are options, not a progression to full autonomy
Task boundaryAgent actionHuman decision
Advice onlyDraft a recommendation without changing a system.A person checks the advice and decides whether to act.
Isolated changeEdit a branch and run tests using limited permissions.A reviewer assesses the change before it enters a shared system.
Pre-authorised routine actionPerform an explicitly permitted action after defined checks pass.An authorised person sets the scope and stop conditions; the team monitors results.
High-impact or uncertain actionPrepare evidence within its permitted scope.An authorised person decides before execution; the agent stops if authority is missing.

Record who delegated the task, its scope, the evidence and the outcome. Protect these records under the applicable data-handling rules. Escalate failed checks, unexpected access requests and changes outside scope.

AIHow AI can help

Given a change and the control’s criteria, AI can assemble evidence links and flag apparent gaps for review. The control owner checks the original results and resolves missing evidence. Retain the findings and authorised decision; a generated summary does not grant approval.

Next step: document one checkpoint’s purpose, required evidence and decision authority. Review the proposed change with the person responsible for that control.

Sources: [5]; [6].

Culture: make learning and accountability visible

People need to be able to question AI output, report failures and ask for help without pressure to demonstrate speed gains. DORA links high trust and effective information flow with stronger software delivery and organisational performance.

Explain the change and listen to concerns

Before a pilot, the team lead can explain its purpose, how responsibilities may change and how results will be assessed and which decisions remain open. Invite concerns about workload, job responsibilities, skills and review effort. Record unanswered questions and assign someone to follow them up.

DORA’s AI Capabilities Model identifies a clearly communicated position on AI use as a supporting capability. Make permitted tools, data boundaries and the route for questions easy to find. Agree these with the relevant organisational owners.

Agree what acceptable work looks like

Set acceptance criteria before the task starts. Use tests for behaviour that can be checked automatically and human review for contextual judgement. An AI-generated assessment can help a reviewer, but it can also be wrong.

For each change, record whether the criteria were met, which risks remain and who can decide on them. Where recovery matters, check the recovery method. Passing tests alone does not demonstrate that a change is useful, secure or ready to release.

Turn failures into improvements

At a retrospective, examine the task instructions, available context, tool permissions and review evidence. Agree a specific improvement, an owner and a completion date. Recognise useful escalation and defects caught during review, as well as successful delivery.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to group permitted pilot feedback and failure reports into themes linked to the original records. Team members check for missing or contradictory accounts, then record agreed improvements, owners and follow-up dates.

Next step: discuss one failed AI-assisted task with the people involved. Choose one improvement to a test, instruction or control, and record who will make it.

Sources: [7]; [8].

Technology: provide bounded access and recovery

Build on existing repositories, delivery pipelines and access controls. Start with the capabilities needed for the pilot; a new platform is not a prerequisite. When an agent can act, make its permissions and actions attributable to the task and the person who authorised it.

OWASP recommends limiting tool functionality, permissions and autonomy, with authorisation enforced by the connected systems rather than the model. Prompts alone are not an access-control boundary.

Check the platform’s support for the task

Suggested capabilities and how to check them
CapabilityPractical check
Relevant contextGive the tool current requirements and approved reference material; record their versions and restrict access to what the task needs.
Identity and permissionsUse scoped credentials or delegated access that preserves the user’s authority limits. Check that unauthorised actions are denied.
Isolated executionSeparate experimental work from shared systems. Limit tool access, execution time and spending.
VerificationRun tests against acceptance criteria and retain the results. If AI assesses the work, compare its findings with qualified reviewers using the method below.
Action recordsRecord changes, tool calls, versions and outcomes with appropriate access and retention controls; avoid unnecessary sensitive content.
RecoveryTest stopping a run, revoking access and restoring affected state. Identify actions that cannot be undone.

To check an AI assessment, select routine and higher-risk cases from the task’s agreed scope. Ask qualified reviewers to assess the original evidence against the same criteria, then compare conclusions. Record missed defects, unsupported findings and unresolved disagreements. The person responsible for the check decides whether the automated assessment is suitable for the proposed use, with additional review where uncertainty remains.

DORA’s capabilities research associates useful internal platforms and access to relevant internal data with stronger AI benefits. This supports improving context and platform quality; it does not justify unrestricted data access.

Build, harden and operate the delivery path

The Platform / Cloud Engineer connects delivery automation with reliable service operation. Agree these responsibilities with the application team and existing platform and security owners:

  • CI/CD pipelines: configure repeatable builds, tests, security checks and deployment stages, with scoped deployment credentials and retained results. Demonstrate that a failed check blocks promotion and rehearse rollback. Use the EDS pipeline stages when applying the EDS workflow.
  • Infrastructure setup and hardening: provision environments through reviewed, version-controlled infrastructure as code, which describes resources and configuration in files. Apply agreed identity, network, secrets and patching controls. Record hardening checks, track configuration drift and test restoration from backups where needed.
  • Operations and application health: work with developers to collect metrics, logs and traces, and check important user journeys. Agree service health targets; monitor availability, latency, errors and resource capacity. Test alert routing to a named responder and maintain runbooks with diagnosis, escalation and recovery steps.

AI tools can draft pipeline definitions, infrastructure changes and runbooks, or summarise operational evidence. Review generated changes and test them in an isolated environment before authorised promotion. Grant agents permissions for their delegated task; agree separately who can deploy, change production infrastructure or respond to incidents.

Supporting guidance: [10]; [11]; [12]. The allocation to a Platform / Cloud Engineer is this guide’s proposed mapping of these practices.

Keep verification independent of generation

Combine automated tests with specialist review according to the task’s risk. An agent’s explanation that its own work is correct is not independent evidence. Review the test cases too: tests generated from a misunderstood requirement may repeat the same error.

A merge request can collect code-change evidence, but other actions need controls at their own point of execution. Data access, deployment and external communications may happen outside a code review. Enforce permissions where those actions occur.

AIHow AI can help

On an isolated pilot task, an agent can draft code and run permitted tests using the supplied context. Developers and platform engineers inspect its actions, test access boundaries and recovery, and retain the results before proposing a wider scope.

Next step: list one agent’s tools, data access and permissions. With the system owner, remove unnecessary access and test recovery.

Sources: [9]; [8].

Ownership: maintain shared capabilities

Squad pilots depend on shared services that need ongoing maintenance. Map the responsibilities below to existing roles, and name an owner and a deputy or support route before wider adoption.

Shared service ownership before wider adoption

Infrastructure and hardeningPlatform / Cloud Engineer, with platform and security ownersMaintain infrastructure code, environment separation, access and network controls, patching, hardening evidence, drift checks and recovery tests.
Operations and application healthPlatform / Cloud Engineer and application service owner, with developersMaintain health signals, dashboards, alerts and runbooks; agree responders, support coverage and escalation. Review incidents and feed findings into delivery work.
Approved modelsModel service owner, working with security, privacy and procurementMaintain permitted models and uses, data terms, access limits and costs; evaluate upgrades and provide migration notice.

State whether the cases assess a development tool or an AI capability in the product; investigate gaps and rerun checks after relevant changes.

Keep development-tool evaluations separate from evaluations of AI behaviour in the delivered product. The upload pilot assesses a development agent; the upload feature itself need not contain AI. If a product does contain AI, name the owner of its behavioural evaluation and operational monitoring as well.

Keep this ownership record with the shared service documentation, including contacts, capacity, funding and review dates. Squad leads report gaps to these owners; service owners publish changes and known limits to affected squads. A pilot lead does not automatically inherit responsibility for the shared platform.

Next step: map the shared capabilities needed by the pilot to existing owners. Record maintenance capacity, support contacts and funding gaps; resolve them with the responsible owners before wider adoption.

Run a pilot and decide from evidence

A pilot is a small trial of a proposed way of working. Use it to find out whether AI helps the team reach an accepted result with an acceptable level of effort, cost and risk. Measure the whole task, including the time spent checking and correcting AI output.

Choose one recurring task whose result you can check and whose failures the team can contain and recover from. Name a pilot lead to collect the results and confirm who is authorised to decide whether the team adopts the workflow.

  1. Record how the task is done today. The pilot lead collects results from comparable recent tasks: completion time, review and correction effort, defects and cost. This is the baseline for comparison. Use the same timing points throughout, such as from an agreed task brief to an accepted result.
  2. Write down the trial boundaries. Record the tool and version, tasks included, permitted data and actions, reviewers and acceptance criteria. Agree when to stop, such as an attempt to access data outside the trial. For a trial affecting a running service, name the application and platform responders and test alerting and recovery before starting.
  3. Agree how to judge the results. Before the trial, the decision owner and relevant reviewers set measurable targets and required checks using the scorecard below. Agree how many tasks to try, how long to watch for defects found after acceptance and who can decide on functional acceptance, security approval and wider adoption.
  4. Run the trial and keep a complete record. The pilot lead records each attempt, including failures, abandoned work and recovery effort. Reviewers compare the results with the acceptance criteria and retain the test and review evidence. Ask participants what helped, what added work and when they needed help.
  5. Compare the results and record a decision. The pilot lead presents baseline and trial results side by side, with links to the evidence and an explanation of gaps. The authorised decision owner uses the rules below to choose the next step. Record the reasons, scope, unresolved issues, follow-up owners and next review date, then share the decision with affected teams under the applicable data-handling rules.

Use the same measures for the baseline and the trial, and show the number of tasks and tool versions. Compare similar tasks separately, noting differences in difficulty, risk and team experience. An overall average can hide a task type that performs poorly. Mark missing evidence as unknown. A small before-and-after comparison can inform the next decision, but cannot show that AI caused the difference.

Suggested pilot scorecard: agree targets before the trial
MeasureWhat to record and check
Tasks comparedDescribe the scope, difficulty and risk of each task type, participants’ experience and familiarity with the repository. Count baseline and trial attempts, including failures, and explain any differences that weaken the comparison.
Useful resultsRecord which results met the acceptance criteria and what shows they helped the intended user. Keep links to tests, review findings or user observations.
Time to an accepted resultMeasure elapsed time from the agreed start to acceptance, including waiting. Record active human effort separately so that a shorter wait is not mistaken for less work.
Review effortRecord time spent checking requirements, generated work and test evidence. Include specialist reviews and repeated review rounds.
Corrections and failed attemptsRecord time spent fixing rejected outputs, rerunning the tool and recovering from failures. Include effort spent on work that never reached acceptance.
Defects and control failuresTrack defects found after acceptance over the agreed observation period. Record severity, user impact, failed security or other required checks, incidents and recovery results. Examine each serious failure individually.
Readiness to run and support the serviceFor changes affecting delivery or a running service, record pipeline failures, infrastructure security findings, availability, response times and errors. Compare alert response and recovery results with agreed targets. Name the operational owner and record gaps before expanding.
Total costInclude tool and model charges, infrastructure, pipeline and monitoring services, setup, training, human work, shared harness maintenance, evaluation, support and incidents. Include failed attempts and count each cost once. Report both total cost and cost per accepted result.
Participants’ experienceAsk about mental effort, interruptions, learning and confidence in questioning AI output. Compare feedback with observed work and requests for help; fewer reported problems may mean problems went unnoticed.

Decide whether to expand, restrict, stop or keep testing

Use the agreed targets and required checks to decide what happens next. The decision owner records which uses the evidence supports, which remain uncertain and what work follows. The options below are suggested decision rules to agree before the pilot.

  • Expand when the results meet the agreed criteria. Check outcomes, quality, total cost and participant experience, including review and correction effort. Complete the agreed period for observing defects and confirm that required controls pass. Before adding users or tasks, confirm funding, service ownership and reviewer capacity. Extend use only to task types and permissions the evidence supports.
  • Restrict use when only part of the trial works well. If benefits hold for some tasks but others create excessive review work, defects or failed checks, narrow the tasks or permissions and restore human checks where needed. Record what needs to change and repeat the relevant evaluation before restoring excluded uses.
  • Stop when the workflow cannot be justified. If evaluated revisions repeatedly miss the targets, a required control cannot be maintained or ongoing cost and support outweigh the benefit, the authorised owner ends its use. Remove the capability’s access and return the work to a supported workflow.
  • Keep testing when a specific question remains. If there are too few tasks, the comparison is weak, follow-up is unfinished or a proposed revision needs evaluation, record what the next trial will test. Keep the trial within its existing limits, assign the additional work and set an end date for the extension.

If a stop condition is met during the trial, stop the affected actions immediately and follow the agreed response and recovery procedure. Reassess the decision after a material change to the model, agent harness or workflow.

Example · fictional upload-feature pilot results

The team from the earlier example compares six baseline changes with six AI-assisted changes of similar difficulty. It had agreed to look for a saving of at least 15 minutes of human effort per accepted change without weakening quality or access controls. The figures below are fictional averages, including effort spent on failed attempts.

Illustrative human effort per accepted change
ActivityBaselineAI-assisted trial
Draft the change60 minutes20 minutes
Review20 minutes50 minutes
Correct and recheck10 minutes20 minutes
Total human effort90 minutes90 minutes

Drafting took less time, but checking and correcting the work used the saving. The comparison shows no reduction in total human effort. It does not establish whether elapsed delivery time, quality or total cost improved; those need their own evidence.

The decision owner records that the effort target was not met and does not expand the trial. The team proposes clearer task instructions and a short further trial within the same permissions. The owner agrees a review date and asks for the full scorecard before deciding whether to adopt the revised workflow. Even if effort falls, results from isolated tests with synthetic documents do not authorise production deployment or wider data access.

Allow for setup and learning costs, and set a review date so a pilot does not continue indefinitely. Higher autonomy is an option, not a success measure; a useful advisory workflow may remain advisory.

Next step: write a short pilot brief covering the task, participants, baseline, boundaries, success criteria and review date. Use the DORA capability guidance to identify supporting improvements, and read the Concepts guide for ways to specify and supervise AI-assisted work.

Supporting evidence: [8].

AIHow AI can help

AI can draft a comparison of pilot task records using the agreed baseline and measure definitions. The pilot lead checks totals, scope differences, review effort and defects against the underlying records, then retains the comparison for the authorised adoption decision.
